These capabilities significantly enhance the analytical foundation of strategic intelligence systems.From a dynamic perspective, Organizational Learning Theory emphasizes the role of knowledge creation, knowledge sharing, and continuous adaptation in shaping organizational performance. AI contributes to organizational learning by extracting insights from large datasets and supporting evidence-based strategy development. By enabling organizations to identify patterns, evaluate outcomes, and refine strategies, AI strengthens adaptive learning processes and promotes innovation-driven growth (Alami & Al-Masaeid, 2025; Sposato, 2025).AI-driven analytics enables organizations to process large volumes of data, identify patterns, and generate predictive insights that improve decision quality and strategic responsiveness (Vincent, 2021; Weiser & von Krogh, 2023). In highly dynamic contexts, AI-based modeling and scenario simulations help organizations anticipate environmental changes and reduce uncertainty in strategic planning. At the same time, research emphasizes that the most effective outcomes emerge when AI-generated insights are combined with human judgment and intuition in decision processes (Vincent, 2021). Consequently, AI-supported intelligence systems enhance strategic agility and strengthen organizations’ ability to respond to emerging challenges and opportunities in omplex environments (Weiser & von Krogh, 2023; Asmar & Al-Rob, 2024). Beyond theoretical explanations, AI-enabled intelligence systems improve knowledge-driven decision making by transforming data into action-able insights that support evidence-based stra-tegic choices (Sikhakolli et al., 2025; Abdeljaber et al., 2025). In addition, AI contributes to operational efficiency by automating analytical processes and optimizing resource utilization, allowing managers to focus on strategic and innovative activities (Okafor & Murphy, 2025). Research increasingly emphasizes the impor-tance of human–AI collaboration, where AI systems augment rather than replace managerial expertise. Human oversight remains essential for interpreting analytical outputs, ensuring ethical accountability, and aligning technological insights with organizational values and strategic objectives (Štrukelj & Dankova, 2025; Alami & Al-Masaeid, 2025). Future research should continue to explore hybrid intelligence models that combine technological capabilities with human expertise to support sustainable and responsible decision making in increasingly complex organizational environments.

title: Navigating technological disruptions: the interplay of AI-based stakeholder engagement, marketing agility, and firm performance
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI)-based stakeholder engagement can enhance marketing agility and improve firm performance, particularly in environments with high technological turbulence. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected through a survey of 335 companies across diverse industries in Australia, using validated scales for AI-based stakeholder engagement, marketing agility, firm performance and technology turbulence. Partial least squares structural equation modelling was used to analyse the data. Findings The results indicate that engaging stakeholders through AI technologies positively influences marketing agility, which in turn enhances firm performance. These effects are amplified in conditions of high technology turbulence. Research limitations/implications This study focuses solely on technological turbulence as a moderating factor. Future research should replicate these findings and explore additional moderating factors to enhance understanding of AI’s impact on marketing dynamics. Practical implications Businesses should invest in and leverage AI to improve interaction with stakeholders, as it can enhance their ability to respond swiftly to market changes and significantly boost overall performance. These implications are especially crucial for firms operating in environments highly disrupted by technological advancements. Originality/value This study bridges literature gaps by highlighting how firms can use AI as a tool to engage suppliers, employees and other stakeholders effectively. This engagement enhances their capabilities to respond to changes in dynamic and disrupted markets. Additionally, this study sheds light on the boundary conditions of these relationships.

title: Employee response to the artificial intelligence threat
journal: Development in Learning Organizations An International Journal
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to review the latest management developments across the globe and pinpoint practical implications from cutting-edge research and case studies. Design/methodology/approach This briefing is prepared by an independent writer who adds their own impartial comments and places the articles in context. Findings Companies become better positioned to exploit the capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) when employees perceive the technology's significance. A positive response from them drives the informal learning that can enhance career resilience and boost overall firm performance. Originality/value The briefing saves busy executives and researchers hours of reading time by selecting only the very best, most pertinent information and presenting it in a condensed and easy-to-digest format.

title: TRANSFORMING MODERN ENTERPRISES THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGIES
journal: International Journal of Engineering Research and Science & Technology
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies of the twenty-first century, fundamentally reshaping the way organizations operate, compete, and innovate. The rapid advancement of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and intelligent automation has enabled enterprises to optimize business processes, improve decision-making capabilities, and create new opportunities for growth. Modern organizations increasingly rely on AI technologies to analyze vast amounts of data, automate routine tasks, predict market trends, enhance customer experiences, and improve operational efficiency. As global competition intensifies and digital transformation accelerates, AI has become a strategic asset that supports organizational agility, innovation, and long-term sustainability. This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence technologies in transforming modern enterprises and explores their impact on organizational performance, management practices, and competitive advantage. The research investigates how AI-driven systems contribute to process automation, predictive analytics, customer relationship management, human resource optimization, and strategic planning. Furthermore, the study analyzes the adoption of AI technologies across various business functions and evaluates their effectiveness in improving productivity, reducing operational costs, and enhancing decision-making accuracy. Through intelligent data processing and advanced analytics, AI enables organizations to generate actionable insights that support evidence-based management and foster innovation. The findings indicate that enterprises implementing AI technologies experience significant improvements in operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, and business performance. AI-powered systems facilitate faster decision-making, improve resource allocation, strengthen risk management practices, and enhance organizational responsiveness to market changes. However, challenges such as high implementation costs, data privacy concerns, workforce adaptation issues, and ethical considerations continue to influence AI adoption strategies. Organizations must therefore develop comprehensive governance frameworks and invest in employee training to maximize the benefits of AI technologies. The study concludes that Artificial Intelligence is transforming modern enterprises by creating intelligent, data-driven, and adaptive business environments. As technological capabilities continue to evolve, AI is expected to play an increasingly critical role in shaping future business models, management strategies, and organizational structures. Future advancements in generative AI, explainable AI, and autonomous decision systems are likely to further accelerate enterprise transformation and contribute to sustainable business growth in the digital economy.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Strategic Decision-Making in Corporations
abstract: The data-driven insights, predictive analytics, and automation capabilities of Artificial intelligence (AI) have made it a transformative factor in corporate strategic decision-making. This research examines how AI affects strategic decision-making processes in companies, as AI-powered tools can cut costs and driving uncertainty, increasing efficiency and ensuring a competitive advantage. Through case study analysis and empirical data across multiple industries, this research delineates crucial factors that govern AI adoption, such as data accessibility, corporate culture, and legal compliance. The study also provides analysis of accompanying challenges, including those surrounding ethics, algorithmic biases, and the role of human-AI collaboration. The results imply that although artificial intelligence greatly improves both the speed of decision-making and the accuracy of decisions, the effectiveness of AI is required balance, expertise, and ethical governance. This research adds to the growing discussion around using AI to inform corporate strategy, which is crucial for practice to advance and helpful to both business leaders and policymakers.

title: Towards Machine Learning as an Enabler of Computational Creativity
abstract: Computational creativity composes a collection of activities that are capable of achieving or simulating behaviors, which can be deemed creative. A frequently articulated criticism for related systems is that the creative capability yet remains with the software designer rather than the computational creative system itself. The rise of machine learning (ML) enables new ways of combining, exploring, and transforming conceptual spaces to achieve creative results. This article demonstrates that the learning occurring within the computational machine through ML enables creative capabilities therein, allowing the computational creative system to be more creative on its own than ever before. Thus, we perceive ML as a key enabler of computational creativity. In this article, we consolidate research from the computer science, computational creativity, and information systems communities, which has been treated separately so far. We build on a framework of human creativity to examine the relationship between creative capabilities and ML mechanisms in ML-based computational creative systems. Specifically, we explicate, which creative capabilities are already established through ML mechanisms in computational creative systems as strengths. Furthermore, we explicate challenges pointing towards further potential of ML-based computational creative systems to enhance the inherent creative capabilities. Our results reveal that ML-based computational creative systems advance the previously static and explicit principles of non-ML-based computational creative systems, yielding creative capabilities on the machine's own, which yet have been in the realm of human actors.Impact Statement—Creativity is a core organizational skill as it enables innovation. With markets becoming increasingly volatile, constant innovation is essential for organizations to create and sustain their economic competitive advantage. Due to the undisputable relevance of creativity for individuals, organizations, and societies, artificial intelligence research has set out to enable creative behavior in computational systems. Especially, ML methods lately became a highly frequented means within computational creative systems. However, while oftentimes applied, ML is seldomly explicitly assessed for its potential to facilitate computational creativity. In this article, we analyze extant computational creative systems relying on ML. The findings serve as a guidance for the design of these systems in various contexts and as pointers for future research to advance the creative capabilities of such systems.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Its Influence on Strategic Management Decisions
abstract: For businesses in today's world, AI has become a game-changer, crucial to business strategy and decision-making, streamlining operations, and driving organizational success. The paper also illustrates the use of Artificial Intelligence in strategic management decisions and discusses the applications of Artificial Intelligence in strategic management like Data Analysis, Forecasting, Risk Management, Resource Allocation, Competitive Intelligence and Strategic Planning. The approach used in this study is a qualitative review approach where the literature and information sources examined in relation to AI and strategic management are extensive, such as scholarly publications, industry reports and literature. It delves into the potential of AI technologies such as machine learning, NLP (natural language processing), predictive analytics, and intelligent decision-making systems to analyze extensive amounts of structured and unstructured data, detect new market trends, and support data-driven decision-making. The results demonstrate the value of AI to support managers' capabilities and skills, such as forecasting, business process optimization, real-time decision-making and innovation and competitive advantage. Furthermore, AI can assist organizations to make better decisions concerning their customers, optimize their supply chain, manage their finances, and plan human resources, all of which will help the company sustain in the long run. However, the study also reveals some potential hurdles to the implementation of AI, such as issues with data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, ethical oversight, implementation expenses, workforce readiness, and the need for clear decision-making processes. The research highlights that AI can assist in human strategic thinking but it can't do it for them, and that strategic decisions should be taken not just by managers and moral judgement, but also by technological intelligence and contextual awareness. The companies that have implemented strategic management activities based on AI are more likely to adapt to the changes in the business and have competitive performance, the paper finds. Some recommendations are the improvement of AI skills, digital leadership, employee upskilling, and governance mechanisms to maximize the strategic use of AI while upholding ethical and responsible application in the organization. The findings of this study will be of great value to managers, researchers, policy makers and business leaders who want to gain insight into the changing dynamics between AI and strategic management in the digital economy.

title: Agile applications of artificial intelligence to apparel industry
journal: International Journal of Agile Systems and Management
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasing its importance in the field of creating value for companies who seek to gain competitive advantage. This is especially true for the online shopping apparel world, in the case of virtual try-on systems. Following this line of thought the theme consumers acceptance of artificial intelligence virtual try-on systems when shopping online apparel came up as a research problem. In this sense this investigation intendeds to study the acceptance by consumers of the virtual try-on artificial systems when buying apparel online according to specific variables previously defined. To assess this, a quantitative approach was used, based on the structural equations model, the partial least squares technique. This research allowed the creation of a new model based on technology acceptance model by including new variables and revealed that the influence of predictive variables on the dependent variable (ATU) is not the same.

title: IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
journal: ACCENT JOURNAL OF  ECONOMICS ECOLOGY  & ENGINEERING
authors: Syed Mohammad Abbas Rizvi Urvashi Verma
abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force reshaping contemporary management practices across organizations worldwide. In an era characterized by globalization, digitalization, and intense competition, organizations are increasingly adopting AI-driven technologies to enhance efficiency, effectiveness, and strategic responsiveness. Technologies such as machine learning, big data analytics, robotic process automation (RPA), natural language processing, and intelligent decision-support systems are fundamentally redefining how managers perform core managerial functions, including planning, organizing, decision-making, controlling, and human resource management. By enabling the processing of vast volumes of structured and unstructured data, AI systems provide real-time insights, predictive capabilities, and enhanced analytical accuracy, thereby improving the quality and speed of managerial decisions. This research paper examines the growing impact of Artificial Intelligence on management practices by analyzing its influence on operational efficiency, strategic planning, resource optimization, performance management, and organizational innovation. AI-driven tools facilitate data-driven decision-making, reduce human error, automate routine managerial tasks, and support predictive planning and forecasting. In operations management, AI enhances process optimization, supply chain coordination, quality control, and cost management through advanced analytics and automation. Similarly, in strategic management, AI supports scenario analysis, market intelligence, competitive analysis, and long-term planning by identifying patterns and trends that may not be easily detectable through traditional analytical approaches. The study further explores the expanding role of AI in human resource management (HRM), which has become one of the most prominent areas of AI application in management. AI-based systems are increasingly used in recruitment and selection through resume screening, candidate matching, and predictive hiring analytics, thereby improving efficiency and reducing time-to-hire. In training and development, AI-powered learning platforms enable personalized learning paths, skills assessment, and continuous employee development. Performance appraisal systems supported by AI offer more objective, data-driven evaluations, while employee engagement tools use sentiment analysis and behavioural data to enhance workplace satisfaction and retention. These developments indicate that AI is not only transforming managerial decision-making but also reshaping the nature of work and employment relationships within organizations. Despite the significant benefits associated with AI adoption, the study highlights several critical challenges and concerns related to its implementation in management practices. Ethical and privacy issues remain central, particularly with respect to data security, employee surveillance, and the responsible use of personal information. Algorithmic bias and lack of transparency in AI decision-making processes raise concerns about fairness, accountability, and trust. Additionally, the increasing automation of managerial and operational tasks has led to apprehensions regarding workforce displacement, job insecurity, and the need for reskilling and upskilling employees. Resistance to technological change, skill shortages, high implementation costs, and inadequate regulatory and governance frameworks further complicate the effective integration of AI in organizations. The research is based on secondary data collected from scholarly journals, industry reports, policy documents, and organizational case studies, allowing for a comprehensive and analytical understanding of the role of AI in modern management. The analysis indicates that organizations adopting AI strategically—rather than reactively—are better positioned to enhance competitiveness, operational agility, innovation capacity, and long-term sustainability. Successful AI integration requires alignment with organizational goals, strong leadership support, investment in employee skill development, transparent and explainable AI systems, and a robust ethical and regulatory framework. The study concludes that Artificial Intelligence does not replace managerial judgment, creativity, or human intelligence; instead, it functions as a complementary tool that augments managerial capabilities. Managers continue to play a critical role in interpreting AI-generated insights, exercising ethical judgment, fostering collaboration, and making strategic decisions that require emotional intelligence and contextual understanding. As organizations increasingly operate in dynamic, uncertain, and complex business environments, AI is expected to play a pivotal role in redefining managerial roles, enhancing decision-making processes, and shaping the future of management practices. The effective and responsible use of AI will therefore be a key determinant of organizational success in the evolving digital economy. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Management Practices, Decision-Making, Human Resource Management, Organizational Performance.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Business Management: Opportunities and Challenges
journal: Journal of Economic, Management and Engineering Research
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern business management, reshaping industries and organizational processes across the globe. From enhancing decision-making capabilities to automating routine tasks and improving customer experiences, AI offers numerous opportunities for businesses to achieve operational efficiency, innovation, and competitive advantage. However, its implementation also presents various challenges, including data privacy concerns, job displacement, integration complexities, and ethical considerations. This paper explores the role of AI in business management by examining both the opportunities and challenges associated with AI adoption. Through a comprehensive review of existing literature and case studies from leading companies across diverse sectors, this paper provides valuable insights into how businesses can harness the potential of AI while addressing its inherent risks.

title: The transformative impact of artificial intelligence on cloud infrastructure management
journal: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences
abstract: This article examines the profound transformation of cloud infrastructure management through the integration of artificial intelligence technologies. Traditional approaches to cloud management, characterized by manual intervention and rule-based automation, have proven increasingly inadequate as environments grow in scale and complexity. AI-driven approaches are revolutionizing core operational functions through predictive resource allocation, autonomous fault detection, intelligent security monitoring, and cost optimization frameworks. The article investigates how machine learning and deep learning techniques enable systems that not only react to events but anticipate them, fundamentally shifting operations from reactive to proactive models. Through a mixed-methods research approach combining qualitative interviews, quantitative surveys, and operational metrics analysis, the article identify both technical performance improvements and organizational impacts across diverse industry sectors. While benefits are substantial, the study also highlights persistent challenges including implementation complexity, data quality issues, skill gaps, and cultural resistance. The article suggests that successful AI adoption in cloud management requires not merely technological implementation but comprehensive organizational transformation spanning people, processes, and governance frameworks. As cloud environments continue to evolve, AI capabilities are transitioning from competitive advantage to operational necessity, redefining the relationship between infrastructure and business value.

title: Artificial intelligence: a catalyst to organizational learning and development in 21st century
journal: Development in Learning Organizations An International Journal
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate how artificial intelligence is changing and promoting organizational learning and development in 21st century. Design/methodology/approach The paper adopted an exploratory study using the open-ended approach of quantum theory, including 55 depth interviews and one focus group discussion with employees representing top-level management, mid-level management and first-line management having mainly an artificial intelligence and organizational learning/strategies background. Findings The finding showed that when AI is strategically placed within an organization, there is opportunity for humans and AI to learn from one another to develop these new capabilities and core competencies that give an organizations added competitive advantage. Research limitations/implications Exploring artificial intelligence in a context at one sector (telecommunication sector), the research results may lack general acceptance because of disparities of AI adoption in other sectors. Therefore, researchers are encouraged to test the proposed propositions further in other sectors. Practical implications The paper includes implications for artificial intelligence sustainability as a tool for organizational learning and strategy. It is observed that AI has increased the demand for managerial skills such as creativity, innovation, troubleshooting, data mining, emotional intelligence, adaptability and problem-solving. The study showed that organizations will need to have an appropriate level of knowledge and skill in AI to be effective in leveraging it as an integral facet of their organizational strategy. Originality/value This study is novel on account of its applicability in AI’s ability to work harmoniously with human employees which can stimulate mutual learning between the two, resulting in a relationship similar to that of a relationship with a teammate or colleague in the workplace which will invariably results into competitive advantage.

title: The Impacts of Artificial Intelligence on Business Innovation: A Comprehensive Review of Applications, Organizational Challenges, and Ethical Considerations
abstract: This review synthesizes current knowledge on the transformative impacts of artificial intelligence (AI)—computational systems capable of performing tasks requiring human-like reasoning—on business innovation. It addresses the potential of AI to reshape strategies, operations, and value creation across various industries. Key themes include AI-driven business model innovation, human–AI collaboration, ethical governance, operational efficiency, customer experience personalization, organizational capability development, and adoption disparities. AI enables scalable product development, personalized service delivery, and data-driven strategic decisions. Successful implementations hinge on overcoming technical, cultural, and ethical barriers, with ethical AI adoption enhancing consumer trust and competitiveness, positioning responsible innovation as a strategic imperative. For practitioners, this review offers evidence-based frameworks for aligning AI with business objectives. For academics, it identifies research frontiers, including longitudinal impacts, context-specific roadmaps for small- and medium-sized enterprises, and sustainable innovation pathways. This review conceptualizes AI as a driver of systemic organizational transformation, requiring continuous learning, ethical foresight, and strategic ability for competitive advantage.

title: A SEM–ANN analysis to examine impact of artificial intelligence technologies on sustainable performance of SMEs
abstract: This study investigates the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on the sustainable performance of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Employing a hybrid quantitative approach, this research combines Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) to examine the influence of various organizational, technological, and external factors on AI adoption. Key factors considered include top management support, employee capability, customer pressure, complexity, vendor support, and relative advantage. Data collected from 305 SMEs across multiple sectors were analyzed. The results reveal that all the proposed factors significantly and positively affect AI adoption, with top management support, employee capability, and relative advantage being the most influential predictors. Additionally, the adoption of AI technologies substantially enhances the economic, social, and environmental performance of SMEs, reflecting improvements in operational efficiency, cost reduction, and social value creation. The ANN results confirm the robustness of the SEM findings, highlighting the critical role of AI in driving sustainability outcomes. Furthermore, the study emphasizes the positive mediation effects of AI adoption on organizational performance, indicating that AI adoption serves as a key enabler in achieving both short-term operational gains and long-term sustainability objectives. This research contributes to the understanding of AI's transformative role in enhancing the sustainable performance of SMEs in developing economies, offering strategic insights for both policymakers and business leaders.

title: The Evolving Influence of Artificial Intelligence on Customer Engagement Dynamics
journal: New Perspective Journal of Business and Economics
abstract: This study examines the evolving influence of artificial intelligence (AI) on customer engagement dynamics, aiming to provide insights into how AI technologies can enhance engagement, loyalty, and trust among consumers. A quantitative research approach was employed with a causal research design. Data was collected from 140 individuals in the Kathmandu Valley, primarily undergraduate students aged 20-29 years, through a questionnaire utilizing a 7-point Likert scale. Correlation analyses were conducted using SPSS software version 23 to analyze the data. The study's findings highlight the transformative potential of AI in shaping customer engagement dynamics. By leveraging AI technologies, businesses can significantly enhance customer engagement and foster stronger relationships, ultimately driving competitive advantage and sustainable growth in an increasingly digital marketplace. The implications of this research suggest that understanding AI's capabilities can empower businesses to develop more effective customer engagement strategies. This presents opportunities for further investigation into the factors influencing the adoption and effectiveness of AI in customer engagement. Overall, this study contributes to the understanding of AI's role in customer engagement within the context of Nepal. Future research can provide valuable insights for businesses operating in emerging markets, informing the development of AI solutions tailored to the specific needs and preferences of local customers. By exploring these dynamics, organizations can better navigate the challenges of customer engagement in a rapidly changing technological landscape.

title: Factors of Managerial Decision-Making in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Managerial decision-making has long been a central concern in management research due to its critical influence on organizational performance and competitive advantage. The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed traditional decision-making processes by enabling data-driven, automated, and predictive capabilities that augment managerial judgment. This study examines the key factors influencing managerial decision-making in the age of Artificial Intelligence, drawing on classical, behavioral, and contemporary management theories. Through an extensive review of literature indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, and TCI databases, the study identifies and categorizes influencing factors at the individual, organizational, technological, and environmental levels. Individual factors include managerial experience, cognitive style, risk tolerance, and ethical values, while organizational factors encompass culture, structure, power dynamics, and information systems. Technological factors such as data quality, algorithm transparency, and levels of automation, along with external environmental factors including market competition, technological change, and regulatory pressures, are also examined. The findings highlight that managerial decision-making in the AI era is best understood as a socio-technical process shaped by dynamic interactions between human judgment and machine intelligence. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on AI-enabled management by providing an integrative framework for understanding decision-making complexity and offers practical insights for managers seeking to balance analytical rigor with ethical responsibility and strategic oversight in AI-driven organizational contexts.

title: Artificial intelligence in agile IT project management: A SWOT analysis
journal: International journal of information systems and project management
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping agile Information Technology project management by introducing automation and intelligent decision support. This study explores the strategic implications of AI adoption within agile frameworks using a SWOT analysis approach. A systematic literature review of 48 peer-reviewed studies was conducted to identify strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats associated with AI integration in agile environments. The findings reveal that AI significantly enhances sprint planning, backlog prioritization, effort estimation, and software testing; resulting in faster development cycles, improved code quality, and better decision-making. However, these benefits require substantial workflow restructuring, investment in technology, as well as workforce upskilling. Weaknesses and threats are identified, but opportunities for scalable automation and hybrid human-AI collaboration look promising for organizations that adopt AI strategically. The study emphasized the importance of Project Management Technology Quotient (PMTQ) as a critical competency for practitioners navigating AI-augmented workflows. By aligning AI capabilities with agile principles alongside robust governance models, organizations can optimize AI for sustained competitive advantage in the digital project economy.

title: Comprehensive Literature Review: Artificial Intelligence and Corporate Culture
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Artificial intelligence has fundamentally transformed how organizations operate, learn, and compete in the modern business environment. Rather than functioning as merely a technological implementation challenge, AI adoption represents a profound cultural and organizational shift that touches every aspect of corporate operations [1]. The relationship between artificial intelligence and corporate culture is multifaceted and reciprocal while organizations must reshape their cultures to effectively leverage AI capabilities, simultaneously, AI technologies are reshaping workplace norms, beliefs, and behaviors [1]. As AI becomes increasingly embedded within organizational frameworks, executives face a critical decision: develop a digital knowledge-powered culture to harness AI's potential, or risk losing competitive advantage in an AI-centric economy [2]. The evidence consistently demonstrates that effective AI implementation requires planning, ethics, and fundamental alignment between technology and corporate culture [3]. This alignment extends across multiple organizational levels from individual roles and group dynamics to organizational strategy and market positioning requiring systematic attention to how AI reshapes jobs, enhances collaboration, and transforms corporate decision-making processes [4].

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Public Health
journal: Journal of Public Health Management and Practice
abstract: Introduction The promise and potential peril of artificial intelligence (AI) have received extraordinary attention recently. Within the public health arena, a range of AI challenges and opportunities present themselves to leaders of programs designed to protect and promote health.1 For example, as noted in a recent Management Moment column,2 leaders now are confronted with the need to advocate more effectively for public health measures, such as immunization. Within this context, AI holds promise as a tool to assist public health leaders to become more effective advocates within the communities they serve. In this current column, we offer a call to action for public health leaders to learn more about AI and to embrace the potential of AI to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of interventions designed to address population health needs. Context As noted in the excellent recent commentary by Bharel and colleagues,1 generative AI holds the potential to transform public health practice in ways never imagined. Since the public health community has been slow to embrace this potential and to explore the uses of AI, we urge public health leaders to begin to explore the role of AI as a fundamental leadership tool in the toolbox of every public health leader. In doing so, leaders may develop the mindset and skillset to use AI to improve program efficiency and effectiveness while addressing the real threats of misinformation and lack of public trust in public health measures. Arming public health professionals with AI tools to assist (not replace) them As leaders explore employing AI tools to support the work of public health practitioners (particularly at the state and local levels), they will face immediate concerns regarding the potential threats to the workforce, particularly in the face of recent projected budget cuts at CDC and elsewhere across the nation’s public health system. Therefore, we encourage public health leaders to thoughtfully consider the use of AI tools in this time of resource reduction and generalized uncertainty across the public health enterprise as ways to assist and not replace public health professionals. As leaders are charged with “doing more with less,” they should explore the potentially transformative impact of AI tools on the daily practice of public health. If leaders choose to explore the potential of AI, education and training should precede the actual use of these tools. Furthermore, use should be framed within a strategic context as advocated by Bharel and colleagues such that AI is used to augment the core capabilities of public health agencies as described in the Public Health 3.0 framework.3 Using this framework which advocates for a broadening of the role of public health organizations within the community, specific use cases can be identified and explored through leader and practitioner education and training. These use cases may include: Improved Communication Improved Organizational Performance Innovative Approaches to Public Health Practice Improved communication Public health leaders are constantly challenged to communicate effectively with the communities which they serve. In this regard, AI may assist in tailoring messages to better reach the audiences within each community by customizing the content of public communications to the literacy level of the intended audience. Furthermore, since AI can adapt communications to those for whom English is not the preferred language, public communications can be crafted to a wide range of languages. Since many now receive information through social media channels, AI can assist leaders as they work to address misinformation on public health matters using social media. As a result, leaders can then tailor communications to the needs of their audiences more effectively. In addition to communicating with the general public, public health professionals must foster the ability to share stories of public health impact with elected officials, particularly at the local level, and advocate more effectively.2 AI may assist by targeting these messages to that audience in ways which will resonate in a more persuasive manner. Improved organizational efficiency and effectiveness The day-to-day practice of public health involves many meetings as noted in a prior Management Moment column4 entitled “Meetings, Meetings and More Meetings.” In that column and in a later column,5 specific tips are offered to enhance meeting effectiveness, including virtual meetings. Now, AI tools can help in a number of ways such as the use of AI to draft meeting minutes. By using AI to draft minutes immediately after a meeting, staff time can be reduced, and the process of sharing meeting minutes can be streamlined. Since much of public health practice may involve the performance of routine tasks, AI may assist public health professionals (but not replace them). By streamlining certain routine work processes (eg, restaurant inspections and other external activities), these front-line workers may be able to perform specific tasks more efficiently. Furthermore, AI may reduce repetitive and boring tasks (eg, manual data entry) by assisting in process automation and the redesign of public health information systems. In the future, AI may contribute to improved management practices, such as delegation and conflict management, which can lead to improved organizational effectiveness. As a result, AI may provide tools for public health leaders to enhance organizational effectiveness. Uncovering innovative approaches to public health practice As noted by Bharel and colleagues,1 AI may contribute to improved data acquisition and management by streamlining certain processes. As a result, these tools may lead to better discovery of health trends in the community using advanced analytics. As noted earlier, these processes may contribute to enhanced approaches to sharing surveillance information with the public and with decision makers. Educating and training the public health workforce In view of these potential uses of AI in public health practice, education and training of the workforce will be essential before embarking upon isolated and ill-considered uses of AI which could result in further resistance to the use of these promising tools. In the past, as new insights emerged to inform public health leaders, initiatives such as the National Public Health Leadership Institute were launched to provide executive education and peer networks on emerging issues.6 The time has come for a similar effort to educate public health leaders to the potential and pitfalls of using AI in the public health arena. In addition to exploring potential use cases, leaders could be educated on legal and ethical issues surrounding the use of AI in public health. In addition to leader education, workforce training in a range of AI tools will be needed. Approaches such as the Public Health Informatics Institute’s Informatics Academy7 have demonstrated the cost-effectiveness and efficiency of distance-based learning systems for public health informatics training. This systematic approach to workforce training could be used to create a new “Public Health AI Academy” designed to train public health professionals in the implementation of an overall strategic plan for AI use in public health practice. A practical approach to training and educating the public health workforce could be to add sessions on AI and public health to the agendas of regular annual meetings and workshops sponsored by national public health organizations (eg, American Public Health Association, Association of State and Territorial Health Officers, and the National Association of County and City Health Officials). CDC could also sponsor similar training and educational opportunities on this topic. Conclusion Now, more than ever, public health practice faces unprecedented challenges. Major threats to the capacity and capabilities of public health agencies are on the horizon. In this context, AI may assist as agencies are called on to “Do More with Less.” To respond to these threats and opportunities, public health leaders must become more familiar with potential applications of AI to the practice of public health. Areas of opportunity include improved communication, improved organizational effectiveness and efficiency, and uncovering innovative approaches to the practice of public health. In addressing this opportunity, AI should be seen as a way to enhance the impact of public health workers and not to replace them. Thus, immediate training and education of the current workforce (as well as those entering the pipeline) will be essential to contribute to enhancing needed knowledge, skills, and abilities. The age of AI is upon us. Public health leaders must rise to the occasion by thoughtfully exploring the potential (and peril) of AI in service to the health of the public.

title: Evaluating The Opportunities and Risks of Artificial Intelligence In Strategic Management and Business Integration
journal: International Journal of Innovations in Science Engineering and Management.
abstract: This study investigates the evolving trends and potential applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in strategic management, particularly under crisis conditions, to stabilize and enhance business competitiveness. It delves into the various areas where AI can be applied in business process management, with a special focus on how innovations driven by machine learning affect the strategic aspects of company operations. The research provides recommendations for securing competitive advantages and optimizing the use of limited resources. The analysis demonstrates the positive impact of AI-driven innovations on business profitability, highlighting the key benefits of AI technologies and the factors propelling their growth. The study examines the role of AI in predictive analysis, aimed at improving strategic management and overall business performance. It also assesses AI's capability to enhance marketing and management functions, and its effectiveness in using Big Data to analyze competitive markets and customer behavior. The synergy between AI and modern CRM systems is explored, emphasizing how AI and machine learning can deliver a personalized customer experience, even amid changing conditions. Furthermore, the paper addresses the key methods for integrating AI into enterprise business models during crises. It reviews the processes and principles of AI adoption within company operations, identifies critical data quality metrics to mitigate risks associated with innovation, and defines the conditions necessary for leveraging AI technologies to create competitive advantages. This enables businesses to swiftly adapt to the negative impacts of external environmental factors on established processes

title: Implementing artificial intelligence in clinical workflows
abstract: FigureIn today's healthcare settings, the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical practices is transforming patient care, and nurse leaders play a pivotal role in this revolution. Nurse leaders must provide “guidance on the ethical, caring and compassionate, and safe use of AI.”1 Although the implementation of AI presents exciting opportunities, understanding the foundational concepts of AI is crucial. This article provides guidance on effectively integrating AI into clinical settings, establishing governance, determining the project scope, adhering to the implementation framework, calculating total cost of ownership (TCO), assessing return on investment (ROI), and other considerations. Furthermore, this article introduces fundamental AI concepts and models, ensuring that nurse leaders have a solid grasp of the technology underpinning these transformative changes. Among the AI models being introduced in different healthcare settings, each solution may have unique applications in nursing practice. It's imperative to emphasize that well-engineered and trustworthy AI design is essential. Well-designed AI models ensure that nurses can confidently harness AI's potential, knowing that these solutions consider human factors in their design, promote justice, mitigate biases, and ensure fairness in patient care, ultimately enhancing the quality of healthcare delivery.1 FOUNDATIONAL CONCEPTS OF AI Following are descriptions of the foundational AI concepts that form the basis of transformative technologies discussed in this article. AI encompasses a spectrum of technologies, each emulating human intelligence in distinct ways. At its core, AI relies on machine learning (ML) algorithms, a subset of AI, enabling systems to learn from data and make predictions.2 Deep learning (DL), a subfield of ML, employs neural networks (NN) inspired by the human brain's structure, enabling extensive data processing to recognize patterns.3 ML, a subset of AI, emphasizes a program's adaptability with new information. ML software discovers improved decision-making methods autonomously, vital in fields like robotics.4 NN, central to ML, represents AI as interconnected layers of algorithms, loosely resembling the human brain's neurons. These algorithms excel at adaptable recognition, like identifying patients to prevent misidentification.5 DL, a subset of ML, employs NNs with numerous layers (sometimes hundreds or thousands) to process features of data that aren't always perceptible to the human eye. It involves multiple layers learning various aspects of the data, providing a comprehensive understanding.6 Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are common in medical image analysis; for example, detecting findings on X-rays and MRIs.7 They're sophisticated NNs in which not all nodes are fully connected, and some nodes perform operations, such as convolutions, pooling, and maximum values. Natural language processing (NLP) enables AI to understand and generate human language, aiding clinical documentation, speech recognition, and chatbot interactions.8Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, are the most sophisticated new application of NLP, with numerous applications in healthcare.9,10 Generative AI (GenAI), including LLMs, holds promise for nursing applications, as it enables AI models to generate plausible, realistic new data using large quantities of source data as input. GenAI could revolutionize the way nurses approach training, education, and even patient care. GenAI can also interact with patients and facilitate the creation of personalized patient-care plans. By analyzing vast amounts of patient data, AI systems can generate tailored interventions, considering individual medical histories, comorbidities, and treatment responses. Nurse leaders can use this knowledge to understand how AI works and its potential applications in clinical workflows, fostering advancements in healthcare. Figure 1 illustrates the relationship among the various AI techniques and applications that can have a role in healthcare.FIGURE 1:: The relationship among AI, ML, DL, GenAI, and NLPOPPORTUNITIES FOR AI TECHNOLOGY IN NURSING Predictive models Predictive AI models empower nurses to anticipate and proactively address patient needs. By analyzing historical patient data, models forecast readmission rates and staffing requirements. They can also alert nurses when patients are showing collective features of impending sepsis.11 Such capability enables targeted interventions to reduce readmissions and enhance patient outcomes. Fennelly and colleagues analyzed clinical data, identifying the critical impact nursing has on reducing readmissions through transitional care programs, patient education, care coordination and communication, nursing interventions, and documentation. They emphasized that by integrating predictive models from standardized terminologies, we can project the number of home-care interventions needed, ultimately reducing hospital readmissions.12 Risk scores AI-powered risk scoring tools could be used to assess patients' risk levels for specific health events in nursing, such as falls and pressure injuries. These tools analyze factors like mobility, nutrition, medical history, and environmental conditions to predict the likelihood of a patient experiencing a fall or developing a pressure injury. Nurses can use this information to create personalized care plans to prevent adverse events. By leveraging AI algorithms, nurses can proactively identify patients at risk and implement targeted interventions, improving patient outcomes and enhancing safety. A multivariable logistic regression model, developed through a retrospective study of 23,806 ICU patients, outperformed the Braden Scale in predicting the risk of hospital-acquired pressure injuries (HAPIs).13 This model, which identified risk factors for HAPIs among adult critical care patients, was validated using a large dataset of clinical variables. It can help in selecting high-risk patients for focused interventions to prevent HAPIs. Rule-based logic AI Rule-based logic AI models offer valuable decision support for nurses. They provide alerts and recommendations based on real-time patient data. For example, these systems can notify nurses of potential patient deteriorations by monitoring vital signs and prompting timely interventions. Escobar and colleagues quantified the benefits of an automated predictive model designed to identify patients at high risk for clinical deterioration, showing improved hospital outcomes, such as reduced mortality, fewer ICU admissions, and shorter hospital stays. The study found that mortality within 30 days after an alert was significantly lower in the intervention cohort compared with the comparison cohort (adjusted relative risk, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.78-0.90; P <.001).14 Internet of things Internet of things (IoT) refers to a network of interconnected devices and systems that communicate and exchange data over the internet. IoT technologies can assist in the assessment and monitoring of patients remotely, which improves the care delivery model. IoT devices can track vital signs, medication adherence, and activity levels, sending real-time data to healthcare providers, which allows nurses to remotely monitor patients, intervene when necessary, and provide timely care, especially for those with chronic conditions. Thomas and colleagues conducted a systematic review and concluded that remote patient monitoring (RPM) interventions are more likely to reduce acute hospital events if designed with patients, providers, and the implementation setting in mind. They identified 31 factors impacting RPM effectiveness, which were synthesized into six key theories for intervention success: 1) targeting high-risk populations, 2) accurately detecting health decline, 3) providing responsive and timely care, 4) personalizing care, 5) enhancing self-management, and 6) ensuring collaborative and coordinated care.15 AI listening/scribe technology and assistants Ambient listening technology simplifies human-machine communication in healthcare, aiding tasks like clinical documentation and patient reminders. For example, nurses can use voice commands to input patient information, update medical records, and record observations, which streamlines data entry, reduces paperwork, and allows nurses to spend more time with patients. Research on ambient listening technology is still emerging, particularly in nursing. Early studies on provider workflows show favorable outcomes, enhancing patient interactions and reducing after-hours clerical work, with positive patient feedback noting improved interactions with physicians.16 Other studies indicate positive trends in provider engagement without compromising patient safety, experience, or clinical documentation, though no significant benefits were observed in patient experience, documentation, or productivity.17 Continuous improvements are necessary, emphasizing direct electronic health record (EHR) integration, accuracy and context understanding, and customized workflow options. It's important that nurses are involved in the development and implementation of this technology as it becomes available to them. Medical robotics Robotics enables AI-assisted surgeries, rehabilitation, and elder care. For example, autonomous robots can transport medications, equipment, and supplies within healthcare facilities. Nurses can focus on patient care while robots handle logistics, ensuring timely access to necessary resources. Ohneberg and colleagues reviewed 39 robotic systems designed for various tasks, including telepresence, safety navigation, and data processing in nursing settings during implementation stages. The primary benefit was enhanced efficiency, permitting the nursing staff to improve quality care. Challenges included buy-in from end-users and integration into production workflows.18 As nurse leaders gain a comprehensive understanding of these AI models and witness their impact in nursing practice, they can confidently steer their teams toward harnessing AI's full potential. Embracing AI technologies in nursing can lead to improved patient outcomes, enhanced workflow efficiency, and ultimately, a higher quality of care. Additionally, continuous process improvement to leverage AI's platform is crucial. By using AI to support direct care nurses and implementing supportive programs, nurse leaders can address practical challenges and enhance the nursing practice. OPERATIONALIZATION OF AI GOVERNANCE The integration of AI into healthcare often begins organically, driven by clinicians intrigued by its potential. However, this grassroots approach can lead to fragmented efforts toward the common goal of AI integration, underscoring the importance of an executive governance committee comprising diverse stakeholders to assess potential AI use cases and proposed solutions.19 This complex process demands thorough planning, stakeholder engagement, and robust governance to navigate intricacies and optimize benefits. It encompasses various tasks, including establishing governance structures, defining project scopes, calculating the TCO and ROI, implementing best practices for AI model deployment, and ensuring accountability and risk mitigation throughout the execution of AI solutions. Furthermore, establishing an AI Working Group (AIWG) or project team is imperative for ensuring operational stability, optimal outcomes, and value measurement in AI deployment. The AIWG should encompass representatives from various domains, including data science, informatics, end-users, regulatory bodies, policy and privacy experts, researchers, administrative leadership, information services, and patients (if applicable) (see Figure 2). Project requests should undergo rigorous evaluation during the intake process, with the AIWG collaborating closely with leadership to prioritize projects aligned with organizational goals. Key components of AI work may involve mapping, measuring, managing, and governing AI-related risks through a structured, four-phase process, concentrating on safety, accuracy, measurability, and sustainability. To address biases and ensure fairness, experts in human factors and diversity, equity, and inclusion are integrated into the AIWG.FIGURE 2:: Human resources critical to AI initiatives in healthcareNurse leaders must be actively involved in all phases of AI implementation to ensure compatibility with nursing workflows and smooth integration into nursing practices.20 Leaders should support healthcare providers by ensuring nurses have protected time for input and participation in AI-related research and innovation. Additionally, addressing ethical implications and challenges associated with AI is crucial. Nurse leaders must navigate questions regarding privacy, data security, bias mitigation, and the impact on nurse-patient relationships. DEFINING SCOPE Defining the scope of an AI implementation project is vital, serving as the cornerstone for its eventual success. One critical aspect involves precisely identifying the issue that the AI solution aims to tackle; without a clear understanding of the problem, developing an effective solution becomes challenging. Nurse leaders are instrumental in this process, conducting comprehensive problem analysis and consulting stakeholders to pinpoint specific challenges or opportunities within the clinical environment that could benefit from AI technology. For example, nurses may identify the need for more precise predictive models to anticipate patient readmissions or aim to streamline documentation procedures using NLP tools or LLMs. Once the problem is identified, it's imperative to articulate clear and measurable objectives for the AI project. These objectives should outline the anticipated outcomes and advantages that the AI solution aims to deliver, such as reducing cognitive burden or enhancing documentation accuracy. Nurse leaders must also consider the technical requirements, resource constraints, and project timeline to assess its feasibility within the existing infrastructure and identify potential obstacles that may require attention. Involving relevant stakeholders, including IT specialists, in the scoping process ensures that diverse perspectives are considered and potential concerns are addressed early on, establishing a robust foundation for the successful implementation of AI projects in clinical settings.21 AI IMPLEMENTATION FRAMEWORK Figure 3 illustrates the phases for AI implementations in a clinical practice setting, including data curation, model development, validation, deployment, and ongoing monitoring. This AI life cycle requires meticulous oversight and adherence to established governance frameworks to ensure the ethical and responsible use of healthcare AI.FIGURE 3:: AI implementationData curation is essential for training AI or evaluating a model for clinical deployment. Developing an AI model typically requires different datasets: training data (examples repeatedly given to the algorithm for it to “learn” and create the model), validation data (optional additional examples to fine-tune the trained model), and test data (previously unseen examples to objectively measure model performance). The test set shouldn't include patients from either the training or validation sets to accurately characterize the model's performance on previously unseen data.22 Carefully collecting and organizing these data reduces the risk of poor or unexpectedly biased model performance. When training the algorithm, an appropriate model architecture should be chosen that optimally fits the input data (for example, images versus text versus signals). Collaboration with diverse stakeholders also ensures that the data accurately reflect the clinical question the model may be tackling (for example, alerting the team to a patient on the verge of decompensation). Models should be tested in the environments where they'll be used clinically, accounting for potential variations across different sites within a healthcare network. It's essential to continuously monitor AI performance with real-world data after the model goes live in the care environment. Mitigation strategies should be implemented to address any detected deviations from expected model performance or biases in model outputs. Such strategies may include temporarily taking the model offline for fine-tuning to improve performance; or limiting the environments in which the model is used, or the patients with whom the model is used, to those environments/patients that minimize bias and maximize performance.
